items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Harry White [Bill Johnson] showed me them four basic things.

ctx.x: So they got the influence from New Orleans.

That’s right, because they was . . . You see, people began to dance to a subtle sort of thing, not a blasting thing, but a bouncing. A heartbeat in the music. That’s what King Oliver had in his music with Baby Dodds and Bill Johnson. They had that old New Orleans funky sound. So that’s what you got. Later on, that’s what musicians all over the country tried to imitate, tried to get that sound. Basie had it, because he’s not a explosive piano player. He plays subtle piano, and he . . . honky tonk and a barrelhouse…
A lot of people think that New Orleans music is real loud and real fast, which is not true.

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: INTERVIEWER: You have to look at Bill Johnson... [INTERVIEWEE] Mmm-hmm.

ctx.x: Those are the ones that migrated to Chicago, migrated from New Orleans around 1915, '16 and '17, and migrated from Chicago to Frisco and Oakland and San Diego. Jelly Roll and all of them went out there, when Watts was... They speak of Watts as a cowboy place, a country...you know, Western town.
That almost makes me the oldest one now standing. After you get past Garland and Pops Foster. I guess you ...(?)... and your day will come. There it is. You have to look at Bill Johnson...
